newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dutch gay union hits 50 with marriage still a goal.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dutch gay union hits 50 with marriage still a goal.

text.p: Fifty years after it was created as a literary club, the world's oldest gay rights organisation says its work is far from complete.

Although the Netherlands never outlawed homosexuality, public opinion was such that founder members of the Centre for Recreation and Culture, formed just after World War Two as a haven for gays, were known to each other only by aliases.

As it prepares to celebrate its golden anniversary, the group -- now known exclusively by its Dutch acronym COC -- has long shed its covert roots to become one of the most vociferous campaigners for gay rights with some 10,000 members.
"There are still laws that need to be changed and there is still discrimination and violence against gays and lesbians here," said COC's deputy director Jop van der Linden.
One of its biggest victories was the lowering of the age of homosexual consent in the 1970s to 16 from 21, in line with that for heterosexuals.
MARRIAGE IS STILL A GOAL
A quarter of a century on, the gay lobby has set its sights on an even more ambitious target -- extending full marriage rights to same-sex couples.
The ruling Labour-led reformist coalition government has already taken several tentative steps towards legislating for gay partnerships.

Recent amendments to Dutch family law which look set to gain majority backing from members of parliament include the national registration of co-habiting couples, which would impose the same rights and obligations as marriage with regard to issues like inheritance and pensions.
The bill, which applies both to same-sex and opposite sex couples living together, will be voted on in parliament later this month and could become law on January 1, 1998.
However, the measures stop short of marriage and offer no remedy to gay couples wishing to adopt children.
"The legal consequences of registration are the same as those for marriage, with the exception of the consequences for any children born from such union," the Justice Ministry said.

A second measure, yet to reach parliament, will introduce legal rights of custody to non-biological parents. However, this too falls short of allowing the so-called social parent to adopt. In short, the child will not be his or hers.
The government has yet to decide whether children will be able to inherit from social parents.
For COC and other groups, this is not enough. Freedom to marry remains the goal.
"Marriage still has to be opened up," said Van der Linden.
OTHER AIMS
COC also wants to see better education, partly to dispel discrimination and partly to ease the process of "coming out".

It also hopes to coax a more liberal attitude from certain conservative pillars of society. One such project is its work with the Amsterdam police to encourage gay victims of violence to come forward.
"There are now more gays and lesbians working in the police which makes things easier," Van der Linden said.
One area COC need hardly address, however, is tourism.
Amsterdam, in particular, has not lost its lustre to gay visitors.
Last month, the International Gay Travel Association led a familiarisation trip to Amsterdam, but acknowledged that the city is already well known to many gay travellers.
"Of our gay clients, 80 percent of those going to Europe will make a stop in Amsterdam at some stage," said one delegate.
The IGTA said that the Netherlands was one of a number of European countries targeting the expanding gay and lesbian market and their so-called pink dollars.
The Dutch national tourist board believes the combination of an acceptance of gays and a lively nightlife is the key to drawing thousands to Amsterdam, often referred to as Europe's gay capital.
"We are a city where there is no gay area of town, every section of Amsterdam is as accepting as the other," said the board's Conrad van Tiggelen.
In 1998, the city's gay-friendly image is likely to be confirmed when Amsterdam hosts the Gay Games.
